generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, a placement or applied project offers what no seminar can: contact with real data, real clients or real research. A few weeks as a research assistant, in a school, or in a clinical team can build practical skills, grow your employability for competitive routes such as clinical or occupational psychology, and show you which part of the field actually suits you. The gains are there, but only for the student who arrives knowing what they want from the time.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students take up the same month-long placement in a research lab.

Tom turns up each day, runs the tasks he is given, and goes home. The data gets entered. But Tom never decided what the placement was for, so it drifts: no goal to steer by, no sense of what to notice about how the study is run, nothing gathered beyond the hours logged. At the end there is little to show but attendance.

Amara starts the same placement with two or three clear aims: to learn how the lab handles ethics and consent, to understand how a study is designed, and to leave with examples for a clinical psychology application. Those aims shape each day, what to volunteer for, what to ask the researchers, what to note. The same month yields skills, insight and evidence.

Both served the same time. Only Amara decided in advance what to draw from it, and so actually drew it.
generatedProse.summary: A psychology placement offers real skills, employability and self-knowledge, but only to the student who aims for them. You can now identify what such an experience can give you, recognise the difference between drifting and drawing value, and set clear aims of your own. The next lesson turns those aims into action: the moves that get the most out of the experience while you are in it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's month more valuable than Tom's?

items.text: She set clear aims in advance, which shaped what she did, asked and gathered.
She was given more interesting tasks than Tom was.
She spent more hours in the lab than Tom did.
She was naturally more confident than Tom.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara set aims in advance, and those aims steered what she did, asked and gathered across the month.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara decided before the placement began.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's month was more valuable because she set clear aims in advance, which steered the whole placement, not because of better tasks, more hours or confidence.
